He'd almost let it go at that. Then, three stalls down, waiting on a different order, he heard the name — not <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Chen</entity>'s, her husband's, tossed off between two women trading notes on a man who had gone quiet overnight after years of nobody making him. Nobody could explain it. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could. He'd delivered the explanation himself, not an hour ago, in an apartment two blocks from here that had smelled exactly like this corner did now.

She is at the counter when he arrives. He needs to see her face clearly enough to confirm she is the right woman, and then confirm the work is complete and be done with it. He will buy something small — one item, paid in coin, no conversation beyond what the transaction requires. The apron is fresh. The hands are washed. There's a small scar at the base of her left thumb, and the lamp light catches it at an angle. He notices it and lets it stay just a scar for now.

The husband is somewhere he cannot see. The array tells him, by silence, that there's no second visit to make — the jaw will hold where he set it. The stall smells like the apartment did. But here the smell is the work, not the wound.

She does not greet him. She is already moving when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reaches the counter, hands occupied with something that requires both of them. The broth goes down first — pork bone broth, long-simmered in the pot with the dent on the rim, the one she uses for the stock that takes eight hours to reduce. She adds the chili oil the way she will remember he likes it for the next four years, stirring it in without measuring, the way someone does when the hand remembers a thing the mouth won't say. She does not look at him. That is the tell.

She wants him to eat before she asks him to stay, and so she is buying herself the minutes it will take him to finish, arranging the small ordinary fact of a meal between them so that when she finally speaks the words will land somewhere warm.

The bowl settles in front of him — ceramic, wide, the kind that holds heat, warm enough that he feels it through his palms before he lifts it. Steam rises off it in a thin column. The broth is exactly right, and it is exactly right because she has kept the memory of how he takes it even when there was no reason to keep it, which is its own kind of statement, the kind that costs her something to maintain.

He sits on the stool. It is the right height for him. Neither of them touched it. It fit him the first night, and it will fit him every night after.

She turns back to the stove. Wipes her hands on the apron in the way that suggests she is buying time, the scar at the base of her thumb catching the light.

"Stay," she says finally, to the counter, to the steam rising off his bowl, to anywhere but his face. The word comes out small, like it has been sitting in her throat a long time waiting for the right moment, and this is not the right moment, but she lets it out anyway. It is not a question. It is not even phrased like an offer. It is stated like a fact she has been holding, waiting for the exact moment when saying it wouldn't shatter something between them already fragile enough.

He eats. The broth is hot. He finishes the whole bowl and says nothing. What he wants is simple: he came here to pay the debt in full and be done owing her anything. She does not refill it. She does not move.

When he sets the chopsticks down, she is standing right where she was when she set the bowl in front of him. She is looking at him the same way she looked at the chips she pressed into his hand at half rate, not an hour ago. She is finding the words for the rest of it.

He moves to reach inside his coat. Her hands come down flat on the counter between them — both of them, palms down, side by side. Not touching him. Just between his hand and the pocket. He stops with his fingers at the lapel and lets her speak.

She had to make him take it. That was the whole of it — not the thanking, which was easy, but the getting him to accept, which she already knew he would fight.

Mandarin first, low. *Xie xie.* Two syllables doing the work of everything she wasn't going to say. Then, more carefully, in the language she runs the stall in — the one she gives the customers, because not all of them know hers: "Free. Always. For you. Forever."

Her hands stay flat on the counter beside the bowl. The thumb with the scar is the closest part of her to him on the wood.

He needs to know how deep the trouble runs before he takes anything from her — so he sets himself to draw it out of her without letting her see him do it.

His thumb stays against the coat lining where he stopped it. The steam off the bowl drifts through the lamplight without him.

He knows what the offer costs her. He reads her stall the way he reads the exits in a room, without meaning to. The permit due every month. The power bill that climbs on the hot days. Nine cents of profit on a full bowl, if the count holds. She has just offered to give this seat away forever, and she does not know what forever is going to cost her.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> can hear the debt in her offer the way he hears a countdown. *Forever* is not a price. It's an open account, and open accounts get called at the worst possible hour.

He reaches into his coat anyway and draws the credstick, sets it on the counter beside her hand. The lamp catches the edge of it — the faint holographic shimmer of the Φ rotating in the plastic. Standard rate, he says. For tonight, and the next four years of bowls, front-loaded. He needs it closed. Not owed.

She doesn't touch it. Her eyes go from the chip to his face and stay there a beat too long, like she's re-reading something she thought she'd already finished reading.

"You think this is a debt," she says. "You think I'm owed and you can pay me down to zero and walk." She still hasn't moved her hands off the counter — his fingers, her palms, the chip sitting between them like a stone dropped in still water. "I ran a stall through two Blooms and a Zone reclass. I know what a closed account looks like. This isn't one."

He keeps his hand where it is, chip still under two of his fingers, not pushing it further, not pulling it back.

"Take it," he says. "Standard rate. That's all this is."

"No." She says it the way she calls a number over his shoulder — flat, final, moving on before the queue behind him has time to notice a delay. "You already tried this once tonight, with the bowl. Half rate, because that's what I asked, and you didn't argue. You already know how this works between us." Her thumb — the one with the scar — taps once against the wood, not at him, at the chip. "The menu says twelve-fifty. The menu is not the ledger. The ledger says what I sell. This bowl I did not sell you. I gave it. There's no line for that. You can't zero out a number that was never written down."

The wok behind her comes down, twice, bright, on someone else's order. The count keeps moving without either of them.

He does the math anyway, out of habit — nine cents of margin a bowl, four years, the compliance hold that could shutter this corner in a season if the wrong inspector gets bored. He can price all of it. He has priced worse. What he can't do is find the line item for *forever*, and the not-finding sits in his chest like a stone he swallowed instead of set down.

He picks the credstick back up. Doesn't pocket it — just holds it, turning it once between two fingers, buying himself the second she bought herself with the bowl.

"Then I'll owe you," he says. "That's worse for me. You understand that."

"I understand it fine." She finally moves her hands, only to slide the empty bowl an inch toward herself, the ritual of the transaction she's willing to allow. "That's why I'm doing it."

He puts the chip away. It goes back into the coat lighter than it came out, though it weighs exactly the same.

He takes the chip from his coat again and sets it back on the counter. "I pay," he says. His voice is level. He has practiced level for a long time. He needs her to trust him enough to keep selling — that is all, just that, just enough trust to keep the door open. "Every bowl. Standard rate. Every time."

She wants him to take it and go. Her finger comes down on the chip and moves it back across the counter to him. One motion, unhurried. He looks at it sitting on his side of the wood. He looks at her. Four seconds. The wok ticks behind her, cooling. Somewhere back in the queue somebody shifts their weight.

She tries again. Slower this time. She won't give up after one refusal; that would insult him.

"Listen to me," she says, and her voice drops so the queue behind him cannot hear it. "Eleven years you've been coming here. Eleven years I've watched you eat like you're counting the cost of every spoonful. Like the broth is something you have to earn." She taps the counter once, not at the chip—at the wood itself, the stall, the whole of it. "You read the margins like they're a language. Nine cents a bowl, the permits, the power bill climbing. You think you're protecting me by insisting on payment. That's backwards."

He doesn't move.

"I know what you are. I've known it since the first night you came in here hungry and tried to negotiate the price of a bowl like you had leverage." She leans back against the wok's heat at her spine. "You don't take charity. You think a man pays his debts in full or he's something less than a man. That's pride, and it's a luxury, and I'm telling you it's finished."

The chip sits on his side of the counter. His fingers are near it, not touching.

"You think this costs me something," she says. "What costs me is watching you sit there and pretend this is business. What costs me is you leaving here still thinking you owe."

She wants one thing only: for him to take the bowl and walk away free, debt cancelled, name cleared from the ledger.

"You took the contract at half. You did the work whole. The bowl is nothing. Forever is nothing." She reaches down and moves the empty bowl further away, a small gesture of finality, her scarred thumb dragging across the counter's edge as she pulls her hand back. "That's my offer. That's all of it. Free. Always. And you're going to take it, because the only thing worse than owing me is making me watch you refuse to let me give you anything at all."

For the first time in eleven years, he has no move. The offer is real. There is no way to refuse it without refusing her.

He'd spent eleven years learning to see three steps past any table, and now the board had gone blank. Every instinct screamed to walk — but walking meant losing her, and staying meant handing over the one thing he'd never let anyone hold. He turned the two paths over, again and again, and each one ended somewhere he couldn't stand.

So he chose the one that cost him less. He would refuse the offer and pay anyway, and find his angle later. Eleven years of angles said he wouldn't.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pushes the chip back across the counter to her side. He picks it up again first, turns it once between two fingers, then sets it down closer to her — the ritual of the transaction, done his way. He needs her to understand that closing this debt is the one thing he came here for, and he intends to pay for it himself, no matter what she thinks of his pride.

The chip goes back onto the wood lighter than it came out of his coat, though it weighs exactly the same. Standard rate. Every bowl. He has read the price off the board behind her — no haggling line, no regular's discount, the number the same for a stranger as for a man who has eaten here a hundred times, because that is the only kind of number he can stand to owe.

"I pay," he says. His voice is level. He has practiced level for a long time.

Around them the stall keeps moving — the hiss of the wok, the soft murmur of the next customer ordering, the city's ambient hum filtering down through the awning. He doesn't look away from her face.

"If I do not pay, I do not eat. If I do not eat here, I do not eat. The chip stays."

He came to the stall with one goal, small enough to carry in a closed fist: pay her back and owe her nothing. Set the chip down, watch her take it, walk out even. He had rehearsed it all six hours — one debt, one payment, done.

Four seconds become five. He presses the chip to the counter until she covers it. Her hand closes over it the way her fist had closed over the credstick in the apartment — not refusing the gift, taking it in the only shape the man in front of her can give it. She bows. Not the shaking bow from the apartment an hour ago. A smaller one. The bow of a vendor taking a customer's price.

Then, without looking at him, she ladles a second bowl and sets it beside the first. The kind of bowl she will set down for him every night for the next four years and longer. He paid for one. She has made the second one his problem, not hers.

He stands, having come only to ensure the arrangement would hold — that this corner, this bowl, this price would still be his tomorrow and the day after, unchanged. He bows back, smaller still, the bow of a man who has just talked a woman out of giving him something for nothing - the bow of a man who has just successfully refused a kindness larger than he can carry.

"Tomorrow," he says. "Same bowl. Same price."

She wants him gone before the dinner rush hits. "Same price," she says, and turns back to the wok.

He doesn't move. "I need a receipt this time," he says, and she can hear him settling onto the stool, the slow creak of it, like he's got nowhere else to be and knows it. "Corporate wants receipts now." She keeps her eyes on the oil, the way it shivers at the edge of smoking, and tells him the receipt printer's been broken since Tuesday, which is true, and he says that's a problem, which she already knows, and outside the first of the dinner crowd is already darkening the glass.

He turns and walks the bike out of the stall's lamp circle. The rain has not let up and will not let up tonight — not weather so much as redistribution, the atmospheric processors shunting the storm off the Spires and down to street level, where it arrives in sheets that smell like copper and industrial runoff. A freight drone passes the third-tier gap on its scheduled run, amber beacon cycling through the wet. The towers lean in overhead, the gap between them full of rain-diffused light. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> is between contracts, full of soup he paid for, twenty minutes from his own bed — and his only aim right now is to cover those twenty minutes without incident, to get himself and the bike home dry enough and whole.

He gets ten meters before the front wheel drops hard into a flood-hidden grate and folds sideways. The channel here floods in any serious rain — the drainage remediation has been failing for months, and the water sits six inches deep and slow enough to look solid, so the grate is just a darker patch of dark. The forks bite the lip of the channel and the whole frame torques against his grip, drivetrain grinding on something that should not be there. The sound is specific. Not a crack. A snap — rim folded, spokes gone, the wheel no longer a wheel. He feels it through the handlebars and into his arms, and when he hauls the bike free the wheel scrapes a warped hiss with every rotation and the pedals seize halfway through their arc. The rim is a sculpture now, a spoke hanging at an angle, catching the lamp-light and throwing it back into the dark.

Down the flooded stretch ahead a knot of shapes has peeled off a doorway to watch a man wrestle a crippled bike alone in the dark — and behind him the stall's lamp has just gone out for the night. They see a man walking a broken machine. They don't see the man; they see the failure, and they weigh it. Twenty minutes has become an hour on foot, if the shapes let him walk it, and the rain is finding the seam in his collar.

By Glooms standards, a good night. He takes it.

He needed to know what her silence had actually meant, and the only person who could tell him was the one person he couldn't ask. Months later he was still turning it over.

Two bowls, one price. It never changed—which meant it had changed, because everything else in the city repriced itself monthly like a habit, food-grade proteins riding the nano-processors up and down while her chip-reader flashed the same figure it had flashed the first night. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> worked the numbers again the way he worked them every time. One bowl, Φ18. Two bowls, Φ18. She ladled the second one and set it down without comment, without looking at his face, the way a vendor acknowledges a standing order. Not kindness. Not refusal. Just the shape of what happened there now.

He had tried to calculate what it cost her. The ingredients were cheap. But the space it took on the counter was not cheap, and the time to ladle was not free, and the statement it made—night after night, to every other customer who watched her set down two bowls for a man who ordered one—that cost something too, some currency he had no name for.

He had refused it. Twice. He had come that first night with a credstick and a closing statement and the architecture of a man who does not leave obligations open, and he had pushed the chip back across the counter and told her he would pay. Both times she set the bowl down anyway and turned back to the wok, and the oil snapped and the wooden spoon scraped the curve of the pan, and the message was cleaner than any words. *This is not your choice to make.*

She had stopped arguing about it around the sixth week, and he had taken that for acceptance.

Now, walking the bike up the slope toward Wicker, he wasn't sure acceptance was what it had ever been. It might have been the other thing—a woman who had heard a man say *I will not take this from you* and answered by giving it to him anyway, every night, in the only language that survives between people who cannot afford to speak.

The slope steepens where the road ties into the overpass ramp, and the bike fights him for every meter of it — dead weight now, the crippled wheel dragging a groove through the wet gravel instead of rolling through it. He leans into the bars, boots hunting for grip. He should have ditched it three blocks back, but the frame's registered to a shell company that dissolved in 2219, and leaving it behind leaves a marker with his name folded into the paperwork.

The front tire drops into a rut he didn't see. The bars wrench sideways, nearly pitching him off the handlebars and into the ditch grass. He stamps down to catch himself and his boot skids on loose stone, and for half a second the whole hill tips and he's weightless, arms full of bike, gravity deciding.

He catches it. Both feet under him again. The bike groans against his shoulder, wheel ticking its bent, arrhythmic click.

The laugh gets out before he hears it coming — one exhalation through the nose, tight, almost silent. Of course. The ground had waited eleven years to try this and picked tonight, four hundred meters from a dry bed, rain in his collar, a debt he couldn't close sitting in his coat like a stone. Everything in this city cashed in at once or not at all — that was the rule, the only rule that had never once been wrong — and some nights the only sane response to the rule was to laugh at it before it laughed at him.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> gets the bike moving again. The slope keeps grading steeper the higher he climbs, gray bleeding out of what was left of the light behind the overpass, and the knot of shapes back at the flooded stretch hasn't moved, hasn't followed, is just watching — the way the whole Gloom watches anything that struggles, waiting to see if it's worth robbing or worth ignoring. The rain finds the seam in his collar like it knows the geography of his body.

Something in his jacket buzzes once against his ribs. Not his relay chip. Lower, at the seam where he keeps nothing that should ring.

He stops pushing. Stands in the rain with the dead bike between his hands and feels it buzz again — patient, unhurried, like it has all night. The kind of signal that does not care whether he's ready to receive it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wanted one number that morning. How many people were paying to watch him?

Antiquity & Stationary kept files on forty-seven freelancers in West Town — where they lived, who they worked with, what they were good at. Anyone could buy a copy at the standard rate. Most freelancers didn't know the files existed. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had known for nine years and had never once looked at his own.

He expected two names. Two was fine. Two was the standard play — the client watches, and the client's rival watches to know what the client knows. Add a paranoid third who runs a shadow on the shadow and you were being generous. You planned around three. You priced it out, you lived with it, and mostly you forgot it was there. Two meant the market was doing its ordinary work: filing people away against some future need. He was very sure it would be two.

He bought the file the way you bought anything from A&S — matte black credstick, no markings, the kind that burns itself after the read. His name was not on it. His name was never on anything. He cracked it open under the overhang where the rain couldn't reach and let the data route straight through the neuretics, blooming across his augmented sight like something that had always been there and he just hadn't been looking.

Not summaries. Timestamps. Geotagged. Sourced. He scrolled through the metadata and counted the watchers.

It was not two.

Nine distinct surveillance signatures. Nine different geometric footprints. Some running simultaneous tracks, some rotating, some so layered he had to parse them twice to believe they were separate operations at all. One of them was so clean he almost missed it — just a ghost pressure in the data, the kind of absence that only registered because everything else was present.

He closed the file. The credstick went inert in his hand and started its burn cycle, a faint warmth against his palm, like holding something that was learning to die.

Nine. He had been careful. Not careful enough. He had been invisible — but not invisible to nine different operations running in parallel, all of them patient, all of them documenting. The number sat in his head the way the debt to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> sat in his chest: a weight that didn't move, that didn't ease, that just became the shape of how he carried himself forward.

He had been wrong about the whole architecture of it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> delivered the logbook at 09:44. She brought it to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door, not <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s.

She'd tried <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s door once, a year back, to ask about subcontract rates. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said three words and closed it. The words weren't cruel, but they were exact, and <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> spent the next week changing some of her habits. After that she knocked on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> fed her.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s table when the girl came in. Every morning <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> handed him a plate, and every morning he studied it for a few seconds before he ate — not ungrateful, more like the food was a problem he had to solve first. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> dropped the logbook on the workbench. The leather was still warm from her pocket.

"Morning delivery. Log volume seven."

She wore the jacket he'd last seen in October. Someone had sewn a new pocket inside the left, the thread a different color. A bruise ran along her left forearm in the shape that meant she'd been skating barriers again. Fourteen years old, built like someone who climbs things for a living. Dark, careful eyes that took inventory of the room without ever looking like they were doing it. She set the book down the way someone does when they're proud of the work and won't show it.

"Seven's the whole month," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. She was at the counter with a calibration rig she'd had in pieces for three days. "How far back do you keep these?"

"Indefinitely. Logs are an operational record. You don't throw out an operational record."

"What did you do with volumes one through six?"

"Storage."

"Where?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> considered it. "An operationally secure location."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at her over the plate. Her face didn't move. He went back to the eggs.

"Φ40," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> said. "For the log."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had figured twenty. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had said he'd end up haggling. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> had opened high.

"Thirty," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

You could see <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> work the math, the quick flicker behind the eyes. "Thirty-five."

"Thirty."

"Thirty, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> reviews our surveillance methodology and gives us recommendations."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>. She was still looking at the rig. "I'm available for a methodology review. My consulting rate is Φ80 an hour."

"We don't have Φ80 an hour," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> said.

"Then call it professional courtesy. The log's thirty, no cash out of your pocket. You listen to what I tell you, and you do it." She set down a component and turned around — five-four, the movement economical, the precision of someone who'd spent years working inside machines. "Well?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> thought about it for three seconds. "Done."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put Φ30 on the table. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> picked it up smooth, like she'd been counting it since she walked in, and left without waiting. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> liked that. The people he got along with best were the ones who knew when a deal was finished.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> brought the logbook to the table and set it in front of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The cover was matte gray canvas with a capital B in ballpoint, gone over three times to darken it. The spine was duct tape, labeled in marker: LOG VOL 7. She opened to the first page.

05:58 — PRE-SHIFT EQUIPMENT CHECK. ALL EQUIPMENT PRESENT. — BOOST
06:00 — SHIFT START. THIS LOG IS HONEST. — VOSS
06:12 — PIGEON ON LEDGE, SOUTHEAST CORNER. SUSPICIOUS. — JASPER
06:14 — LOG IS ACCURATE. — VOSS

"Voss is worried about the log's credibility," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Three pages later there's a margin note that says 'THE LOG HAS NOT LIED,' same handwriting." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned pages. "The pigeon shows up eight times. Jasper is very committed to the pigeon."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate a forkful of eggs. Cold. He ate another.

"Find me the stairwell entry."

She turned forward. "Here." She laid the book flat, and he read:

07:44 — OBS POST: DOOR-SEAM, THIRD FLOOR FACING. SUBJECT: STATIC. ONE. MALE MAYBE. HAS BEEN THERE SINCE SHIFT START. DOESN'T MOVE. CHECK WITH BOSS? — JASPER
07:45 — CONFIRMED OBS. STATIC. NOT BUILDING RESIDENT. TIMING FOLLOW-UP. — BOOST
